title: Al-Ghaniyy, the Self-Sufficient
tomorrow: rich, or content? why does one verse put the two side by side?

cards: Dadi prays every day, again and again, to a God the Qur'an says needs nothing at all. That was yesterday's question, and a king holds the answer. Solomon, Sulayman in Arabic, is in his court.
He asks who can bring him the throne of the queen of Sheba, from far away. One says: before you rise from your seat. Then someone with knowledge of the Book says: before your gaze returns to you.
Solomon looks. And the throne is standing right there in front of him. What does a king say when the impossible just arrived?

teach.h: THIS IS FROM THE BOUNTY OF MY LORD.
teach.b: Not "look what I did." In the Qur'an's telling, Solomon says this is from the bounty of his Lord, a test of whether he'll be grateful. Then he adds the part that answers Dadi's question.

teach.h: THANKS IS FOR YOUR OWN SOUL.
teach.b: Whoever gives thanks gives it for the good of his own soul, and whoever is ungrateful, his Lord is free of need and generous. That's today's Name. Al-Ghaniyy, the Self-Sufficient, needing nothing.

teach.h: YE ARE THE POOR. HE IS THE ABSOLUTE.
teach.b: Another verse says it to everyone, in Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Ye are the poor in your relation to Allah. And Allah! He is the Absolute, the Owner of Praise."
So the prayer isn't a payment that keeps the world running.

There's a hadith qudsi, words the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave as from God, that says if every person who ever lived, first to last, had the heart of the most devout among them, it would add nothing to His kingdom.
Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: in Solomon's own words, thanks is for the soul that gives it. Dadi's prayers don't fill a need in God. They do something in Dadi.

how: Muslims describe prayer as worship offered for God's sake that, in the Qur'an's words, is for the good of the worshipper's own soul.

o: the Rich One, owner of all gold
the Distant One, too far to care

games.q: the throne and the thank you — tap the pairs.
p: the one with knowledge of the Book
before your gaze returns to you
gives it for his own soul
ye are the poor in relation to Allah

s: the Qur'an says people need God, and God needs nothing from them
"Ye are the poor in your relation to Allah. And Allah! He is the Absolute, the Owner of Praise."
Solomon says the throne came because of his own power
he calls it the bounty of his Lord, a test of whether he'll be grateful.
prayer in Islam is a payment God needs to keep the world running
a hadith qudsi says all creation's devotion would add nothing to His kingdom.

games.q: you thank your grandmother for dinner, and she waves it off: 'i don't need thanks.' do you still say it?
o: no; if she doesn't need it, saying it is pointless.
yes; like Solomon's thanks, it does something in the one who says it.
only when she looks like she actually wants to hear it.
games.why: Solomon said whoever gives thanks gives it for the good of his own soul. the thanks isn't only for the receiver.

practice: Close your eyes and set down the feeling of owing a performance. Nothing you bring to the next two minutes is needed by anyone. Simply breathe, and notice what a sit feels like when it isn't a payment.

wordCard.voice: Al-Ghaniyy. The Self-Sufficient: needing nothing from us, which is why every thank you lands back on the one who gives it.

orig.note: Arabic: the Self-Sufficient, a Name of Allah; Pickthall renders it 'the Absolute' in 35:15.

carryVoice: Here's one for the pocket: he needs nothing, so your thanks is a gift to your own soul. See you tomorrow.
